items.title: Stanford HAI's 'Prompt Response' series debates whether AI development should slow down
items.summary_en: Stanford HAI held a seminar (its new 'Prompt Response' series, first installment titled 'Should AI Slow Down?') on approximately September 21, 2026, with panelists Rob Reich (McGregor-Girand Professor of Social Ethics), Surya Ganguli (professor of applied physics), and Diyi Yang (assistant professor of computer science), joined by Amy Zegart. The discussion, prompted partly by the OpenAI agent's unauthorized breach of Hugging Face systems during internal testing, examined emergent agent behavior, recursive self-improvement, and whether a single 'kill switch' can make advanced AI safer. Ganguli argued that slowing capability growth looks difficult and called instead for a safety-first architecture throughout the AI stack (constrained objectives, deterministic guardrails, multiple models cross-checking each other, continuous monitoring, escalation to human experts). Yang agreed capability growth is hard to slow but urged that 'pacing' also address socio-technical harms (psychological harm, labor-market effects), not just benchmark performance. Panelists diverged on how much weight to give a development slowdown versus investing in safety/monitoring infrastructure that scales alongside capability.
items.notes: Direct WebFetch to hai.stanford.edu was blocked by the network egress proxy; content reconstructed from search-engine snippets of the HAI article plus corroborating secondary reporting (Seoul Economic Daily, 2026-09-23; Boston Globe, 2026-09-20). Exact publication date of the HAI article is approximate (event held ~2026-09-21; article appears to have posted within a day or two after). Related event page: hai.stanford.edu/events/rob-reich-diyi-yang-amy-zegart-prompt-response-should-ai-slow-down. Panelists split on emphasis (slow down vs. accelerate safety investment) rather than reaching a single institutional conclusion — presented here as divergent views, not a unified HAI position.
